curso.subtitulo: Code agents in the terminal with opencode · 84 minutes

agentes.subtitulo: An agent is model + prompt + permissions
puntos: Build has unrestricted access: edits files and runs commands.
Plan is the same model with edit and bash denied. Not dumber: it has its hands tied.
Tab doesn't toggle two fixed modes: it cycles through all primary agents you have configured.
The mode field accepts primary, subagent or all. If omitted, it's all.
Subagents are invoked with @, and work in their own context.
permission.task decides which subagents each agent can call.

equipo.subtitulo: Write how your team works and keep it in the repository
puntos: orchestrator: coordinates and delegates. Has edit denied, so it can't do it itself.
architect: defines structure, components and types. Doesn't write code either.
developer: the only one with hands. And the most constrained: doesn't expand scope or add dependencies.
reviewer: validates and ends with a verdict, PASS or CHANGES REQUIRED. Who reviews, doesn't fix.
What makes it work isn't the prompt, it's permissions: an instruction can be ignored, a permission can't.
The cost is real: slower and more expensive. Worth it for large tasks, to separate design from execution, and to have an uncontaminated review.

revision.subtitulo: Your work shifts from writing code to reviewing it
puntos: Layer 1, the diff: did it touch files you didn't expect? Did it add dependencies? Are edge cases covered?
Layer 2, ask for accountability: have it summarize what changed and why. Don't reconstruct it by hand.
Layer 3, a reviewer without hands: with edit denied it reviews and can't fix, and arrives without the biases of the conversation where the code was written.
Without configuring anything: Tab to Plan and ask from there. Same effect.
/undo reverts the agent's last change. If it went down a path you don't like, undo and rephrase.
Permissions prevent it from doing it, the diff and the reviewer let you see it, /undo lets you remove it.

reglas.subtitulo: The agent doesn't fail because it's dumb, it fails because it's uninformed
puntos: AGENTS.md is a markdown file in the repo root that's always loaded in context.
/init generates it by reading the project. What it produces is a good draft, not the truth: open it and fix it.
Put the project's quirks, the stuff a newcomer takes two weeks to discover. Don't put the novel: it takes up context in every request.
It's committed, so the whole team works with the same rules. And so do the agents.
Precedence: the project's going up the tree, then the global, and CLAUDE.md as last resort. First one found wins.
The project's for team rules; the global only for your personal preferences.

documentacion.subtitulo: The agent writes the documentation and the documentation improves the agent
puntos: Documenting is the task with the best effort/result ratio: the agent can read the whole project.
Documentation lives in docs/, versioned with code, and reviewed in the same MR as the change.
With instructions you hook it as context, and it accepts paths, URLs and globs.
Keeping it up to date is something that must always happen, so its place is an AGENTS.md rule, not a command.
The cost of that rule: it loads on every request and applies to trivial changes too.

codigo.descripcion: The instructions field wires docs/ in as context

comandos.subtitulo: The body isn't fixed text: it's a template
puntos: A markdown in .opencode/commands/. The filename is the command name.
The frontmatter has description, and optionally agent or model. The body is the prompt.
With shell syntax in backticks, opencode runs the command and pastes its output in the prompt.
With @file it's replaced by the file's content.
With $ARGUMENTS, $1 or $2 goes what you type after the command.
That's why /commit knows what you changed: you don't tell it, git diff brings it inside the prompt.
Committing is the perfect command example because it's your decision: you launch it when you want.

codigo.descripcion: Frontmatter, shell output and $ARGUMENTS in a single command

skills.subtitulo: Procedures the agent loads when it sees they apply
puntos: Reusable instructions the agent discovers and loads on demand. Native support, no plugins.
At first it only sees the name and description; if it fits, it calls the skill tool and then loads the content.
The description is the only thing it sees before deciding: write it thinking about when to activate it, not what it contains.
The frontmatter name must match the folder name.
The rule: if it always applies, AGENTS.md. If you launch it, command. If it sometimes applies and the agent can recognize when, skill.
Good examples: adding a translated string, preparing a release, an accessibility checklist. Procedures with steps, that don't always apply.

rag.subtitulo: Retrieve only what's relevant and inject it in the prompt
puntos: Instead of feeding the model everything, you retrieve what's needed and put it in the prompt.
The twist: code agents barely use vector RAG with embeddings.
They do agentic search with grep, glob and read: they search like a developer would.
It works better for code, because there's structure and exact names, not fuzzy similarity.
The three real forms of retrieval in opencode are instructions, skills and MCP.

mcp.subtitulo: A model has no hands. MCP gives it some
puntos: A standard for giving the agent new tools without the vendor programming them.
Configured in three lines: remote by URL, or local by command.
With Playwright the agent drives a real browser: opens your app, interacts and tells you what it saw.
That turns "trust me, it works" into a real check: it's another review layer.
The most valuable from day one: browser, up-to-date docs and GitLab.
